questions.stem: He was so tired that he fell asleep ___ he reached home.

options.option_text: until (until = up to a point in time; 'fell asleep until he reached home' is illogical)
before (correct: 'fell asleep before he reached home' — he fell asleep prior to arriving ✓)
after (wrong: 'fell asleep after reaching home' changes the meaning — the point is he was so tired he slept earlier)
while (while = simultaneously; you can't fall asleep while reaching home in standard sense)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The sentence emphasises extreme tiredness — he fell asleep BEFORE even arriving home. 'Before' is the only preposition that captures this meaning. 'While' is close but grammatically awkward ('fell asleep while he reached home' is unnatural).

options.option_text: for (wrong: 'insist for' is not standard — 'insist on' is the correct collocation)
on (correct: 'insist on' = emphasize or demand; 'insisted on punctuality' ✓)
at (wrong: 'insist at' is not a phrase)
about (wrong: 'insist about' is not standard English)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Insist on (something/doing something)' is the correct collocation. Other insist collocations: 'insist that + clause' (She insisted that he was wrong). Do not confuse with 'persist in' (doing something), 'emphasise' (no preposition needed).

questions.stem: Neither the captain nor the players ___ responsible for the defeat.

options.option_text: are (wrong: with 'neither...nor', verb agrees with the noun closest to the verb — 'players' is plural, so 'are' seems logical, but 'nor the players' makes 'players' the subject closest → 'are' is actually correct here!)
were (past tense — wrong if we assume present context)
is (wrong: verb should agree with 'players' which is plural)
was (past singular — wrong)

questions.explanation: A is correct. With 'Neither...nor' / 'Either...or', the verb agrees with the NOUN CLOSEST to it (proximity rule). Here, 'players' (plural) is closest to the verb → 'are'. If it were 'Neither the players nor the captain ___', the answer would be 'is'. Rule: verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.stem: She has been living in Mumbai ___ 2018.

options.option_text: for (wrong: 'for' is used with a duration — 'for 6 years'; 2018 is a point in time, not a duration)
since (correct: 'since' is used with a specific point in time; 'since 2018' = from 2018 until now ✓)
from (wrong: 'from...to' is a pair; 'from 2018' without 'to' is incomplete)
during (wrong: 'during 2018' means throughout the year 2018, not from 2018 to now)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Since' + specific point in time (since 2018, since Monday, since 5 p.m.). 'For' + duration (for 6 years, for three days). Rule: Present perfect tense sentences use 'since' for points and 'for' for periods.

questions.stem: The committee has not yet reached ___ on the new policy.

options.option_text: a decision (correct: 'reach a decision' or 'come to a decision' = decide; 'decision' is the right noun ✓)
a conclusion — also works but 'decision' is stronger here
an agreement (agreement is possible: 'reach an agreement' is valid but 'decision' fits best with 'on the new policy')
a verdict (verdict is used in judicial/legal contexts — policy decisions use 'decision')

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Reach a decision' is the standard collocation for committees or groups making a choice on a matter. Collocations with 'reach': reach a decision, reach a conclusion, reach an agreement, reach a consensus. Verdict is specifically for courts.

questions.stem: Despite working hard, he could not ___ the exam.

options.option_text: pass through (wrong: 'pass through' means to travel through a place)
clear (correct: 'clear an exam' is the standard Indian-English collocation for passing/qualifying an exam ✓)
win (wrong: you 'win' a competition, not an exam)
achieve (wrong: 'achieve the exam' is not standard; 'achieve success in' or 'pass' would work)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Clear an exam' = pass/qualify an exam. This is standard Indian-English usage tested frequently in Bank/SSC exams. You 'clear' an exam, 'win' a match/competition, 'pass' a course.

questions.stem: The news ___ shocking for everyone in the office.

options.option_text: were (wrong: 'news' is uncountable and takes a singular verb)
was (correct: 'news' is singular (uncountable) — 'the news was shocking' ✓)
are (wrong: same error as 'were' — news takes singular)
have been (wrong: present perfect for a completed past event is contextually off)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'News' is an uncountable noun that looks plural but takes a singular verb. Rule: 'The news IS good today.' Similarly: 'mathematics IS', 'physics IS', 'the United States IS' — these look plural but take singular verbs.

questions.stem: He was accused ___ theft by his colleagues.

options.option_text: for (wrong: 'accused for' is not standard)
of (correct: 'accuse someone of (doing) something' is the fixed collocation ✓)
with (wrong: 'accused with' is not standard English)
by (wrong: 'by' introduces the agent, not the crime; 'accused of theft by colleagues' — 'of' comes first)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Accuse someone of something' is the correct collocation. Similar pattern: 'charged with', 'blamed for', 'convicted of', 'suspected of'. Note: in the sentence, 'by his colleagues' is the agent; 'of theft' is the charge.

questions.stem: If I ___ you, I would not have made that mistake.

options.option_text: was (grammatically: 'If I was you' is informal but accepted; formal requires 'were')
were (correct: subjunctive mood after 'if' for hypothetical/contrary-to-fact: 'If I were you...' ✓)
am (wrong: simple present doesn't fit this hypothetical structure)
had been (wrong: past perfect is used for 3rd conditional — past unreality; 'if I were' is 2nd conditional)

questions.explanation: B is correct. This is the 2nd conditional (hypothetical present/future): If + past subjunctive (were), would + infinitive. 'If I were you' uses the subjunctive 'were' for ALL persons (I/he/she/it), not 'was'. This is a very commonly tested grammar point. 3rd conditional (past unreality): If + had + V3, would have + V3.

questions.stem: The children ___ playing in the park when it started to rain.

options.option_text: played (simple past — doesn't show ongoing action when rain interrupted)
were playing (correct: past continuous shows ongoing action interrupted by a sudden event ✓)
have played (present perfect — wrong tense for past narrative)
had played (past perfect — implies the playing was completed before the rain, which changes the meaning)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Pattern: Past Continuous + when + Simple Past = ongoing action (past continuous) interrupted by a sudden event (simple past). 'Were playing' (ongoing) when 'it started to rain' (sudden event). This tense combination is heavily tested in Bank/SSC grammar sections.
